blocks.text: Vehicle Wrap File Types and Image Sizes: What Your Printer Actually Needs

blocks.alt: Vehicle Wrap File Types and Image Sizes: What Your Printer Actually Needs

blocks.html:
Vehicle wrap file types are the single biggest reason a wrap project either moves straight into production or sits waiting on artwork. Send a clean vector logo and properly sized images, and our design team starts laying out panels the same day you approve the quote. Send a logo pulled off your own website, and you are looking at a recreation step, a revised timeline, and a wrap that never quite looks as sharp as the one you pictured.

This guide covers which formats work, how large your images need to be, and why a file that looks perfect on your laptop falls apart across sixteen feet of cargo van — written for the business owners, fleet managers and marketing leads we work with across Etobicoke, Toronto and the GTA.

Why Vehicle Wrap File Types Decide Your Print Quality

A vehicle wrap is one of the largest things your brand will ever be printed on. A logo occupying two centimetres on a business card might occupy two metres on the side of a Sprinter. That is roughly a hundredfold enlargement, and no printer compensates for artwork that lacks the detail to begin with.

Format matters for a second reason unrelated to resolution. Wrap panels are split, nested and repositioned to fit a specific vehicle, so our designers need to move your logo off a door handle, scale it up for a box truck and shrink it for a Transit Connect — without redrawing it. Editable vehicle wrap artwork makes that a five-minute change. Flattened artwork makes it a rebuild.

Vector vs. Raster: The Distinction That Governs Everything

3M’s artwork submission guidance draws the line clearly. Raster art is built from tiny squares called pixels, and when raster images are enlarged too far their edges become jagged and more visible, with quality measured in DPI. Vector art is made from mathematical curves and arcs defined as coordinates, producing precisely defined shapes that enlarge and change without losing visual quality. 3M’s conclusion is direct: vector artwork is preferable for printing because of its resizing abilities.

Where Vector Is Non-Negotiable

Logos, wordmarks, icons, lettering, stripes and anything with a hard edge should be vector. These are the elements a viewer’s eye lands on first, and the ones that look worst when they degrade. A pixelated phone number on a plumbing van undoes the credibility the wrap was meant to build.

Where Raster Is the Right Call

Photographs cannot be vectorised without losing what makes them photographs. Product shots, team portraits, food imagery for a catering van — these stay raster. That is not a compromise; it is the correct tool. The only requirement is that pixel dimensions are large enough at final printed size. Most real wraps are hybrids: vector brand assets sitting on raster imagery in one layered document.

The File Formats We Accept, and What Each Is For

3M lists PDF, EPS and TIFF as its recommended file types for printers. In practice we work with a wider set, because the file leaving your marketing agency is rarely the file that goes to the RIP.

FormatTypeBest used forWhat to watch.AIVectorThe master logo and layout fileLinked photos must be packaged, not just referenced.EPSVectorOlder logo assets from a previous agencyOften contains live fonts; needs outlining.PDFVector and rasterFinal print-ready submissionDown-sampling on save quietly destroys image quality.SVGVectorWeb logos, simple marksGradients and effects can shift in print software.TIFFRasterHigh-resolution photography, flattened artVery large files; no editable text.PSDRaster, layeredPhotographic compositionsKeep text layers live; do not rasterise them.JPG / .JPEGRaster, compressedReference photos of your vehicleLossy; no transparency; rarely print-grade.PNGRasterScreen graphics onlyUsually low-resolution RGB pulled from a website.HEICRasterPhone photos of the vehicleNever suitable as artwork

That last group still has a job: when you request a free estimate, phone photos of your van, truck or trailer in JPG, PNG or HEIC help us assess panel layout, body lines and existing graphics. They just are not artwork.

Image Size and Resolution: How Big Is Big Enough

This is where most confusion lives. “300 DPI” is not a property of a file — it is a relationship between pixel dimensions and printed size. A 300 DPI image at 10 cm wide becomes a 30 DPI image at 100 cm wide. The pixels did not change; the print size did.

3M’s method for checking whether an image can be enlarged is to multiply the final output height by the required resolution, then divide by the height of your original artwork. That gives you the enlargement factor the image can survive.

Resolution by Viewing Distance

Resolution requirements fall as viewing distance grows, because the eye resolves less detail further away. These ranges reflect general large-format practice and are the starting points our design team works from.

ApplicationTypical viewing distanceWorking resolution at final sizeWindow graphics, laptop and helmet wrapsUnder 1 m150–300 DPICar doors, van side panels, storefront decals1–3 m100–150 DPIBox truck sides, trailers, fleet vehicles in traffic3–10 m72–100 DPIHighway trailers, building wraps10 m and beyond30–72 DPI

General large-format industry practice, not a manufacturer specification. Confirm targets for your job with our design team.

Building Files at Scale

Full-size wrap files are enormous — a single van side at 100% can run into gigabytes, slow to open, edit and load into the RIP. 3M recommends setting up files to print at 100%, and where artwork is too large at full scale, using half or quarter scale with the scale factor in the file name, such as “HoodWrap_Half Scale.pdf”. Naming the scale sounds trivial, but it prevents an error that is expensive to discover after printing.

Colour: CMYK, Pantone and the 80 Percent Problem

Your brand colours are almost certainly defined in RGB or Pantone. Wraps print CMYK ink on vinyl. Those are different colour spaces with different limits, and the gap is where colour disappointment originates.

3M’s guidance is specific: use GRACoL 2013_CRPC6.icc or Printwide 2020.icc for CMYK and Adobe RGB (1998) for RGB, call out spot colours explicitly in the file, and remove unused swatches from the palette. On matching, the honest position is that the best digital printers reach only about 80 percent of the PANTONE spot colour gamut, so when a colour is critical a press check should be run for the customer to review and sign off before full production.

If your brand lives on a specific corporate blue or safety orange, tell us at the quoting stage. One more detail worth knowing: standard black is 100% K ink, while rich black is C:60 M:40 Y:40 K:100. The two look identical on screen, but on a large black panel the wrong one reads flat and washed out.

Both major film manufacturers publish ICC profiles for this reason. 3M maintains a downloadable ICC colour profile selector matched to media, RIP and printer combinations, and Avery Dennison’s vehicle wrap bulletin directs printers to use the correct ICC profile and RIP settings, with a recommended maximum ink laydown of 250 percent to avoid excessive solvent buildup in the film. Colour management at this level is a documented, controlled process — part of what you are paying a certified shop for.

Vehicle Wrap Artwork Requirements: The Prep That Prevents Reprints

A file can be the right format and resolution and still fail. These preparation steps come from 3M’s print-ready guidance and our own production experience in Etobicoke.

  • Outline your fonts. Convert text to outlines in Illustrator or InDesign — but do not rasterise fonts in Photoshop. An un-outlined font we do not have will substitute silently.
  • Send the font files anyway. 3M recommends including the original font file, which lets us make late text edits without rebuilding the layout.
  • Flatten your effects. Transparency and drop shadows can look good on screen but produce unintended results in print, so reduce, flatten and expand them where possible.
  • Delete unused layers. This reduces file size and the risk of the wrong elements printing.
  • Watch your gradients. Gradients built over a shorter tonal range band more often than those over a longer range, and banding across a two-metre panel is very visible.
  • Turn off down-sampling when saving a PDF, and package everything — fonts, linked images and supporting assets.

Designing for a Vehicle, Not a Rectangle

Print-ready is only half the job. Wraps have to survive contact with a real vehicle, and that changes layout decisions.

Vehicles have door handles, fuel doors, rubber mouldings, deep recesses and body seams. Avery Dennison’s bulletin is explicit that vehicle graphics are not designed to adhere to rubber or plastic, and that areas such as window moulding and vents should not be covered. Critical content — your phone number, website, certification marks — cannot sit where it will be trimmed out. Panels also need overlap: Avery Dennison specifies at least 0.5 in (13 mm) between overlapping multi-panel decals, so a logo is not sliced across a seam.

3M’s fleet graphics guidance adds the attention dimension: you have three to five seconds to direct a viewer’s eye to the part of the wrap that matters most. That should drive how large your primary message is — the same reasoning behind our guide to choosing fonts readable at 100 km/h.

If you run more than one vehicle, 3M notes that a design working on a semi-trailer may not work on a delivery van, so tailoring to each vehicle type improves effectiveness. That is why we build fleet artwork as a scalable system rather than one fixed file — the principle behind consistent fleet branding across the GTA.

What Happens When You Don’t Have the Right Files

Most businesses in Toronto, Mississauga, Brampton and Vaughan arrive with a logo somewhere between “perfect” and “a JPG someone emailed in 2014.” Both are workable. They carry different timelines.

What you haveWhat we doEffect on scheduleVector logo (.ai, .eps, print PDF) plus brand coloursDrop straight into the vehicle templateNone — design starts immediatelyVector logo, no colour referencesMatch from the file, confirm with youMinimal; one extra approval stepHigh-resolution raster logo onlyManual redraw as vectorAdds design hours before layoutLow-resolution web logo (PNG or JPG)Full manual recreationLongest path, and the most commonPhotography below required resolutionSource alternatives or reshootDepends on available images

Manual recreation is a real design service, and logos with custom letterforms or fine illustration take longer than simple wordmarks. Ask whoever designed your logo for the vector files before requesting a wrap quote. If they no longer exist we will rebuild them, and you will own a proper vector master that pays for itself the next time you order signage, uniforms or a second vehicle.

Keeping those source files also makes future edits cheap. Businesses that hold onto layered vehicle wrap artwork can update a phone number without redoing the whole wrap, because we reprint one panel instead of designing a new one. The same applies to AI-generated imagery: we have printed excellent AI-designed wraps, but generated images are raster and often capped well below wrap dimensions, so the file has to be produced at usable size from the start.

Get Your Vehicle Wrap File Types Right Before You Print

Sorting out vehicle wrap file types before design begins is the cheapest quality improvement available on any wrap project. It costs nothing, it shortens your timeline, and it is the difference between a wrap that looks professional at three metres and one that looks approximate.

At Vinyl Wrap Toronto, our in-house graphics team handles this end of the job for you. We work from manufacturer vehicle templates, print on premium 3M and Avery Dennison films, and back every installation with a three-year warranty against peeling, bubbling and fading. If your artwork needs rebuilding, we will say so upfront rather than printing something that disappoints you.

Frequently Asked Questions

  1. What is the best file format for a vehicle wrap?

    Vector formats. Supply logos and text as .AI, .EPS or a print-ready PDF, with photographs separately as high-resolution TIFF or PSD. 3M lists PDF, EPS and TIFF as its recommended file types for printers. If you can send only one file, a properly saved PDF preserving vector data is safest.

  2. What resolution do I need for a vehicle wrap?

    It depends on final print size and viewing distance, not a single number. As a general guide: 150–300 DPI for close-viewed graphics like window and helmet wraps, 100–150 DPI for van and car panels, and 72–100 DPI for box trucks and trailers. Resolution is always measured at final printed size.

  3. Can you use a JPG or PNG for a car wrap?

    Sometimes, but rarely for the main artwork. Either can work for a photographic element if its pixel dimensions are large enough at full print size. Logos and text supplied this way almost always need redrawing as vector, because web-optimised images lack the detail to enlarge.

  4. Do I need to convert text to outlines before sending wrap artwork?

    Yes, if you are working in Illustrator or InDesign — outlining prevents fonts substituting on our system. Send the original font files alongside the artwork too, so we can make text edits later without rebuilding the layout. Do not rasterise fonts in Photoshop.

  5. Will my brand colours print exactly as they look on screen?

    Not exactly. Screens display RGB light; wraps print CMYK ink on vinyl, and the best digital printers reach only around 80 percent of the Pantone spot colour gamut. If a colour is brand-critical, ask for a printed sample and sign off before full production. We do this routinely for fleet clients across Ontario.

  6. What if I don’t have a vector version of my logo?

    We can recreate it. Our in-house design team redraws raster logos as vector artwork, which adds design time before layout but produces a permanent master file usable for signage, uniforms and future vehicles. Ask your original designer first — the vector file often still exists.

  7. What files should I send with a wrap quote request?

    Your vector logo, brand colour references (Pantone or CMYK values), any photography you want included, and three or four photos of the vehicle, including both sides and the rear. Phone photos in JPG, PNG or HEIC are fine here. Tell us the year, make and model so we can pull the correct manufacturer template.
